recall_prompt: Say how you would find n when n C 4 is 210.
insider_note: Clear the 4! first: n(n − 1)(n − 2)(n − 3) = 210 · 24 = 5040, then write 5040 as four consecutive factors, 10 · 9 · 8 · 7. n is the largest factor, 10 — not the smallest.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Clear the 4! and factor
steps.margin_note: First mark. ⁿC₄ = n(n − 1)(n − 2)(n − 3)/4!. Multiply 210 by 24 to get 5040 = 10 · 9 · 8 · 7.

recall.must_convey: That n C 4 is the product of four consecutive numbers over 4 factorial, so the product equals 210 times 24 = 5040, which is 10 times 9 times 8 times 7.
accept: n C four is n into n minus one into n minus two into n minus three over four factorial, so the product is two ten into twenty four which is five thousand forty, that is ten nine eight seven
multiply two hundred ten by twenty four to get five thousand forty and write it as ten times nine times eight times seven
the product of four consecutive numbers is five zero four zero
two ten into twenty four five thousand forty, adi ten nine eight seven

steps.why: A combination is a product of consecutive numbers divided by r!. Multiplying back by 4! recovers the product of consecutive numbers, which can then be matched.

steps.label: Compare and state n
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The largest factor is 10, so n = 10.

recall.must_convey: That comparing the products gives n = 10.
accept: compare with ten nine eight seven so n is ten
the largest factor is ten so n is ten

steps.why: The product of four consecutive numbers increases with n, so only n = 10 fits; the check ¹⁰C₄ = 210 confirms it.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to check that ¹⁰C₄ really is 210.
